bibliographic.title: Governing Generative AI in Healthcare: A Normative Conceptual Framework for Epistemic Authority, Trust, and the Architecture of Responsibility
bibliographic.citation_apa: Akgün, F. E., & Akgün, M. (2026). Governing generative AI in healthcare: A normative conceptual framework for epistemic authority, trust, and the architecture of responsibility. Healthcare, 14(8), 1098. https://doi.org/10.3390/healthcare14081098

methodology.method_family: normative conceptual analysis with structured literature synthesis
methodology.study_design: essay proposing a normative conceptual framework (ETR Architecture) derived from philosophical principles, ethical theories, and empirical evidence identified via structured searches of PubMed, PhilPapers, and EUR-Lex (January 2020–March 2026)
methodology.sample_description: literature from philosophy of medical knowledge, ethics of trust and testimony, and moral philosophy of responsibility; no primary empirical sample described in provided text
methodology.technology_context: large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT integrated into healthcare for clinical documentation, diagnostic support, discharge summaries, and clinician–patient messaging

eligibility.decision_rationale: The article directly addresses governance of LLMs in healthcare through a normative framework linking epistemic authority, warranted trust, human oversight, verification tiers, accountability, and regulatory transition (EU AI Act, WHO guidance). It matches the review scope on generative AI governance in regulated conversational/clinical AI contexts.
eligibility.manual_spotcheck_reason: Only front matter and pages 1–2 were provided; full framework components, limitations, and complete methods should be verified in the complete PDF.

appraisal.notes: Appropriate normative conceptual method for the stated aim. Objectives and four framework outputs are clearly articulated. Search databases and date range are reported, but detailed search strategy, selection criteria, and limitations are not visible in the excerpt. Framework proposes testable hypotheses but empirical validation is not shown in provided pages.

cerqual.explanation: Highly relevant and internally coherent normative governance framework for healthcare LLMs, but confidence is moderated because only partial text was available and the framework's empirical grounding and full analytical process are not fully documented in the excerpt.

open_codes: EU AI Act high-risk medical AI
coding.theme: Normative governance of generative AI/LLMs in healthcare
coding.subtheme: Epistemic authority, trust, and responsibility architecture (ETR)
rq_alignment: trust and epistemic authority in conversational/clinical AI outputs

synthesis.main_claim: Healthcare governance of LLMs must jointly resolve what kind of knowledge LLM outputs represent, when trust in them is justified, and who bears responsibility when AI-informed decisions cause harm, via an integrated Epistemic Authority–Trust–Responsibility (ETR) Architecture rather than isolated ethics topics such as bias, privacy, and accuracy alone.
synthesis.contribution: Proposes the ETR Architecture with four outputs: a four-tier classification of LLM outputs matched to verification requirements; the concept of the 'epistemic placebo' (governance appearing compliant without genuine oversight); conditions for justified trust; and four testable hypotheses with associated research designs.
synthesis.limitations: unclear in provided excerpt; full limitations section not available in supplied pages
synthesis.use_in_review: Use as central conceptual evidence for normative governance of LLMs in healthcare, especially tiered verification, critique of superficial human-oversight declarations, warranted trust, responsibility/accountability, and alignment with 2025–2027 regulatory transition under the EU AI Act.

evidence.claim: Article focuses on LLM governance in healthcare with explicit LLM/ChatGPT context
evidence.excerpt: Large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT are rapidly being integrated into healthcare for tasks ranging from clinical documentation to diagnostic support.

evidence.claim: Research type is normative conceptual analysis synthesizing philosophical and empirical literature
evidence.excerpt: The framework was developed through normative conceptual analysis—a method that constructs governance proposals by synthesising philosophical principles, ethical theories, and empirical evidence.

evidence.claim: Literature identified via structured searches across named databases and date range
evidence.excerpt: The literature was identified through structured searches of PubMed, PhilPapers, and EUR-Lex (January 2020–March 2026)

evidence.claim: Framework produces tiered LLM output classification with verification requirements
evidence.excerpt: a four-tier classification system that distinguishes LLM outputs—from administrative drafts to clinical evidence claims—and matches each tier to appropriate verification requirements

evidence.claim: Generic human oversight can be an epistemic placebo lacking genuine safeguards
evidence.excerpt: Generic ‘human oversight’ declarations can function as ‘epistemic placebos’ that create the appearance of safety without genuine safeguards.

evidence.claim: Epistemic placebo formally defined as governance appearing compliant without operative oversight
evidence.excerpt: the concept of the ‘epistemic placebo’, formally defined as a governance measure that creates a documented appearance of compliance while lacking at least one operative element of genuine oversight

evidence.claim: Three integrated governance questions on knowledge, trust, and responsibility
evidence.excerpt: What kind of knowledge does an LLM output represent in clinical reasoning? When is a clinician’s or patient’s trust in that output justified? Who bears responsibility when an AI-informed decision leads to patient harm?

evidence.claim: Conversational/clinical use cases include patient messaging and diagnostic support
evidence.excerpt: When a large language model (LLM) such as ChatGPT drafts a discharge summary, suggests possible diagnoses, or replies to a patient’s message on behalf of a clinician

evidence.claim: Regulated high-risk healthcare AI and EU AI Act transition context
evidence.excerpt: the EU Artificial Intelligence Act, which classifies certain medical AI systems as ‘high risk’ under Annex III, will become fully applicable between 2026 and 2027

evidence.claim: Oversight intensity should match clinical risk of each deployment
evidence.excerpt: Healthcare institutions need explicit governance frameworks that match oversight intensity to the clinical risk level of each AI deployment.

evidence.claim: Deploying LLMs without output classification risks vendor-set governance norms
evidence.excerpt: deploying LLMs without explicitly classifying their outputs and building appropriate oversight risks allows governance norms to be set by technology vendors rather than by evidence-informed, patient-centred policy
